tEn: Paid-Growth Alpha: Hector Serrano on Scaling WhisperFlow with UGC
tZh: 付费增长秘籍：Hector Serrano 谈如何用 UGC 规模化 WhisperFlow
sEn: Hector Serrano shares the tactical playbook behind WhisperFlow's 30x revenue growth, from paid UGC and creator programs to cutting through the noise in B2B SaaS marketing.
sZh: Hector Serrano 分享 WhisperFlow 实现 30 倍营收增长背后的战术手册，涵盖付费 UGC、创作者计划以及如何在 B2B SaaS 营销中脱颖而出。

consensus.en: Product-market fit is the only real growth hack; paid and organic amplify, not create, demand.
consensus.zh: 产品市场契合是唯一真正的增长黑客；付费和自然渠道放大需求，而非创造需求。

consensus.en: Performance-based UGC with smart retainers builds a loyal creator roster and scales ad output.
consensus.zh: 基于绩效的UGC加上智能底薪，能建立忠诚的创作者团队并扩大广告产出。

consensus.en: Treat creators as humans and build community; best relationships win long-term.
consensus.zh: 把创作者当人看并建立社区；最好的关系才能赢得长期胜利。

consensus.en: Hire young, hungry creators with proven social growth over pedigree; give them time to fail.
consensus.zh: 雇佣年轻、有社交增长证明的创作者，而非看重背景；给他们时间失败。

consensus.en: Founder-led content humanizes the brand and compounds trust, making paid cheaper over time.
consensus.zh: 创始人主导的内容让品牌更人性化并积累信任，随时间推移降低付费成本。

consensus.en: YouTube is the highest-leverage platform; packaging and long-form team matter most.
consensus.zh: YouTube是杠杆最高的平台；包装和长视频团队最重要。

contrarian.en: Best marketers are allergic to AI; avoid AI for final creative output to cut through noise.
contrarian.zh: 最好的营销人员对AI过敏；避免在最终创意产出中使用AI，以穿透噪音。

contrarian.en: Start paid ads early, even pre-PMF, to learn faster about messaging and conversion.
contrarian.zh: 尽早开始付费广告，甚至在产品市场契合之前，以更快学习信息和转化。

contrarian.en: Creators with no following outperform influencers; they feel more genuine and drive better results.
contrarian.zh: 没有粉丝的创作者比网红表现更好；他们感觉更真实，带来更好的结果。

contrarian.en: Don't give creators detailed briefs; let them experiment freely to produce unique, high-performing ads.
contrarian.zh: 不要给创作者详细的简报；让他们自由实验，以制作独特、高表现的广告。

contrarian.en: Ugly, boring ads often outperform polished ones for technical or older audiences.
contrarian.zh: 对于技术或年长受众，丑陋、无聊的广告往往比精美的表现更好。

contrarian.en: Don't chase volume with AI automation; quality and purpose cut through noise more easily.
contrarian.zh: 不要用AI自动化追求数量；质量和目的更容易穿透噪音。

turns.en: Hector, thank you so much for being here. And welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Hector，非常感谢你来到这里。欢迎来到播客。

turns.en: Thank you. Thank you. I'm excited to be on.
turns.zh: 谢谢。谢谢。我很兴奋能来。

turns.en: I'm even more excited to have you here. What I want to try to do with this conversation is create a very tactical guide to what is working in growing a B2B SaaS product right now. You have been doing this insanely incredible job growing WhisperFlow over the past couple years. I saw this stat that revenue at WhisperFlow grew 30x in the past year, which is absurd. You guys recently raised at something like $2 billion in a very competitive market. Clearly you figured something out. You've started to share some of the strategies that you've been deploying on X. And so we're going to be going deeper into the stuff that you've seen work. First of all, give us kind of a sense of what it is you're responsible for at WhisperFlow. It's kind of your job there and what do you work on?
turns.zh: 我更兴奋你能来。我想通过这次对话，创建一个非常战术性的指南，介绍目前增长 B2B SaaS 产品行之有效的方法。过去几年，你在增长 WhisperFlow 方面做得非常出色。我看到一个数据，WhisperFlow 的收入在过去一年增长了 30 倍，这太离谱了。你们最近在一个竞争激烈的市场中融资约 20 亿美元。显然你们找到了方法。你已经开始在 X 上分享一些你正在部署的策略。所以我们将深入探讨你看到有效的那些东西。首先，请给我们介绍一下你在 WhisperFlow 负责什么。你的工作是什么，你主要做什么？

turns.en: First of all, I just want to give a lot of credit to the other members of the team. Like what I touch at the end of the day is a very small part of the business. And that's mainly content as a whole. I'm a content creator myself and that's how I originally came into Whisper and that role obviously evolved a lot and now I'm kind of in charge of our paid UGC program on the actual content side. I'm not on the media buying side of things. And then on top of that also managing our organic channels for our founder like YouTube and Instagram.
turns.zh: 首先，我想非常感谢团队的其他成员。我最终接触的只是业务中很小的一部分。主要是整体内容。我自己就是一个内容创作者，这就是我最初加入 Whisper 的方式，这个角色显然演变了很多，现在我在内容方面负责我们的付费 UGC 项目。我不负责媒体购买方面。除此之外，还管理我们创始人的自然渠道，比如 YouTube 和 Instagram。

turns.en: Okay, awesome. Something that I've noticed about you and something that I think is really rare these days is you're very good at breaking through the noise. Both in the content you create, like your tweets recently have just gone crazy viral on Twitter. Everyone's sharing it all over my feeds. So clearly you figured out how to do that yourself. Also with the ad work that you do, the UGC work that you do, also very effective. So there's a lot that we can all learn from you and what you've figured out. So just kind of zooming out first, talk about the growth levers that you have been spending time on. What has been working recently in growing WhisperFlow that can work for other B2B SaaS products.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我注意到你的一点，也是我认为现在非常罕见的一点，就是你非常擅长突破噪音。无论是你创作的内容，比如你最近的推文在 Twitter 上疯传。大家都在我的信息流里分享。显然你自己找到了方法。还有你做的广告工作，你做的 UGC 工作，也非常有效。所以我们可以从你和你发现的东西中学到很多。所以先宏观地谈谈你一直在花时间的增长杠杆。最近在增长 WhisperFlow 方面哪些有效，并且可以适用于其他 B2B SaaS 产品。

turns.en: I think the first one and it's maybe a bit corny to say, but I think most importantly Whisper has grown at the rate it has because of the product. It's everything I've been product led growth since the beginning. I joined at the pre-product stage and I remember we had a few thousand users early on and just I don't know where it just started catching steam and like 6 months in I remember Tanay said he was like, "Wow, we really found PMS." Like he found like we struck gold. And then from there just adding on all these other channels, whether it be organic, paid, everything is just adding more fuel to the fire. And what we found a lot of success with through trial and error doing a bunch of different things, me testing a bunch of channels, other people testing a bunch of channels. Like one of the main ones we've landed on now is paid and we're funneling that with a lot of UGC content and we have a lot of pillars inside of paid, whether that be UGC video, statics, influencers, in-house videos, founder storytelling. But yeah, paid ads as a whole, whether it be through meta, LinkedIn, YouTube, etc. has definitely become one of our main pillars at Whisper and it's one of the things I'm leading on the content side of things.
turns.zh: 我认为第一个，也许说起来有点老套，但我认为最重要的是 Whisper 之所以以这样的速度增长，是因为产品。从一开始就是产品驱动增长。我在产品前期阶段加入，我记得早期我们有几千用户，然后不知怎么就开始加速，大约 6 个月后，我记得 Tanay 说：“哇，我们真的找到了 PMF。”就像他发现了我们挖到了金矿。从那时起，添加所有其他渠道，无论是自然流量还是付费，一切都只是火上浇油。我们通过反复试验、做各种不同的事情、我测试一堆渠道、其他人测试一堆渠道，发现了很多成功。比如我们现在主要依赖的一个是付费广告，我们将其与大量 UGC 内容结合，我们在付费广告中有很多支柱，比如 UGC 视频、静态图片、网红、内部视频、创始人故事讲述。但总的来说，付费广告，无论是通过 Meta、LinkedIn、YouTube 等，已经成为 Whisper 的主要支柱之一，也是我在内容方面领导的事情之一。

transcript.secZh: 增长杠杆与产品驱动增长

turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so let's dive in there, but first and I think to your point, it's really important to say none of this will really work if your product isn't exactly great, if there's not real organic product market fit already. I imagine this can work for a little bit and then it just fades away if the product isn't great. So, I guess is that just like step lesson one, this needs to be working on its own with before you start investing in paid?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，那我们就深入探讨，但首先，我认为正如你所说，非常重要的一点是，如果你的产品不是非常好，如果还没有真正的自然产品市场契合，这些都不会真正起作用。我想这可以奏效一段时间，但如果产品不好，就会消失。所以，我想这是不是第一步教训，在你开始投资付费广告之前，产品需要自己运转起来？

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I have like a lot of founders sometimes reach out or or come by the office or or friends and they're like, "What's the hack? Like how did Whisper grow so fast?" And it's like no disrespect to other products, but it's like if you're not having that growth early on and you having to force it a little bit too much and maybe you have to like go back to the drawing board a little bit and like rethink how you're actually positioning the product. Is it actually valuable to your users? It why isn't it growing by itself organically? And like yeah, there's really no hack besides having a good product and then adding more more levers to pull from.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我有时有很多创始人联系我或来办公室或朋友，他们会问：“有什么窍门？Whisper 怎么增长这么快？”这并非对其他产品不敬，但如果你早期没有那种增长，你不得不强迫它太多，也许你需要回到绘图板，重新思考你如何定位产品。它对用户真的有价值吗？为什么它不能自然增长？是的，除了拥有好产品，然后添加更多杠杆，真的没有窍门。

transcript.sec: When to Invest in Paid Channels

turns.en: So, let me ask, when do you think it makes sense to start investing in these in organic channels?
turns.zh: 那么，我问一下，你认为什么时候开始投资这些自然渠道是合理的？

turns.en: Well, I think paid is actually one of the best channels to invest on early on and I learned this from Matt, who's actually our ex-head of growth at Whisper.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为付费广告实际上是早期最好的投资渠道之一，我从 Matt 那里学到了这一点，他实际上是我们 Whisper 的前增长负责人。

transcript.sec: Paid acquisition as a learning engine

turns.en: He's now at Victor, and a lot of his lessons—and lessons that I've learned from him—involve taking this e-commerce approach to SaaS. A lot of companies are scared to turn on the paid engine, but when you actually turn on the paid engine, you learn a lot faster: does the messaging actually resonate with your audience, are you actually able to convert this cold traffic into users? At the end of the day, most companies aren't that skilled in organic content because it's something very new. Unless you have really young people on your team who understand these organic channels really well, know how to package it, know how to make the content, it's really hard to get any clear numbers on whether your product actually has legs, whether people actually resonate with it, whether you're actually able to track these conversions, etc. So I think paid makes sense from the get-go—obviously testing within your limits and the budgets that you have. But if you're able to see that you can turn this cold traffic into paying users, then you have a clear signal that this same messaging or this product will also work on organic if you optimize things a bit more.
turns.zh: 他现在在 Victor，他的很多经验——也是我从他身上学到的——就是把这种电商打法用到 SaaS 上。很多公司不敢开启付费投放引擎，但当你真正开启付费投放引擎时，你学得快得多：你的信息是否真的能打动受众，你是否真的能把冷流量转化成用户？说到底，大多数公司并不擅长自然内容，因为这是很新的东西。除非你团队里有真正懂这些自然渠道的年轻人，知道怎么包装、怎么做内容，否则你很难拿到清晰的数据来判断你的产品到底有没有戏、人们是否真的买账、你能否追踪这些转化等等。所以我认为从一开始就做付费投放是合理的——当然要在你的极限和预算范围内测试。但如果你能看到自己能把冷流量变成付费用户，那你就有了一个清晰的信号：同样的信息、同样的产品，只要再优化一下，在自然渠道上也能行得通。

turns.en: I want to come back to that—what that early team may look like, even maybe pre-product-market fit. But what's really interesting about what you're sharing here is that paid has been around for a long time: running ads on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, all these things. There's nothing new as a platform. And what you're saying here is there's still a lot of alpha and opportunity to grow substantially and do something different in paid.
turns.zh: 我想回头再聊这个——早期团队可能是什么样子，甚至可能在产品市场契合之前。但你分享的内容真正有意思的地方在于，付费投放已经存在很久了：在 Instagram、Facebook、TikTok 上投广告，所有这些。作为平台没什么新鲜的。而你说的是，付费投放里仍然有很多 alpha 和机会，可以大幅增长、做出不一样的东西。

turns.en: Yeah, 100%. A lot of times people also get scared because they'll say, "Oh, I don't want to turn on the paid engine yet or spend a bunch of money because then we're going to reach a point where we oversaturate this market or this ICP." But at the end of the day it's just about getting smarter with how you're positioning the product, and there are always new ways—new messaging, new ICPs you can target—and you won't really reach saturation if you're savvy enough with the angles you're approaching your content with, or how you're approaching that paid mechanism, I guess.
turns.zh: 是的，百分之百。很多时候人们也会害怕，因为他们会说：“哦，我还不想开启付费投放引擎，或者花一大笔钱，因为那样我们会到达一个点，把这个市场或这个 ICP 过度饱和。”但说到底，这只是要更聪明地定位产品，而且总有新办法——新的信息、新的 ICP 可以瞄准——只要你对内容的切入角度、或者对如何操作付费投放机制足够精明，你其实不会真正触及饱和。

transcript.sec: Organic UGC and the Tobin experiment

turns.en: Okay. So let's actually dive into this. Let's talk about paid UGC and paid in general. What's the overall strategy that you have employed that has worked so well?
turns.zh: 好。那我们真正深入聊聊这个。聊聊付费 UGC 以及付费投放整体。你采用的、效果这么好的整体策略是什么？

turns.en: I think it would be good to start maybe from what we learned previously, actually. So where do we go back to? I think this was early 2025—we had an intern named Tobin. He's a good friend now. I don't know if you've heard of him; he also went pretty viral a while back. He ended up joining Polymarket. But basically, Tobin came on as an early intern marketing hire. He didn't really have any experience besides some basic UGC. I think he was studying finance and wanted to be a lawyer. He came in and we just gave him a budget and were like, just throw stuff at the wall, see what sticks. He did a few projects, nothing really worked. And then he found really good success with organic UGC. This was also around the Clue era, when there weren't that many people doing it successfully.
turns.zh: 我觉得也许从我们之前的经验讲起比较好。那要回到哪儿呢？我想是 2025 年初，我们有一个叫 Tobin 的实习生。他现在是我的好朋友。不知道你有没有听说过他，他之前也挺火的。他后来加入了 Polymarket。基本上，Tobin 是作为早期的营销实习生进来的。除了会一些基础的 UGC，他其实没什么经验。我记得他学的是金融，还想当律师。他进来后，我们就给了他一个预算，说你就到处试试，看什么能成。他做了几个项目，都没什么效果。然后他在自然 UGC 上取得了非常好的成功。那也正好是 Clue 时代，当时成功做这件事的人还不多。

turns.en: Explain organic UGC. What is that exactly?
turns.zh: 解释一下自然 UGC。那到底是什么？

turns.en: Yeah, so organic UGC is basically: you get a bunch of creators in a group. These creators will make videos about your product and then post them on their own Instagram pages or their own TikTok pages. So imagine you join Whisper's organic UGC group and you make an account called Lenny Whispers, and then you just upload your videos into there, and then you get paid based on a CPM metric. So maybe it's, I don't know, $2 per thousand views, and then it tapers off as you get higher and higher. Tobin set that up for us, and I think in about two and a half months it was 500 million views. Super low CPMs, and it worked decently well. But I think it was also early on in the organic UGC phase, where everyone was really focused on vanity metrics, and they didn't necessarily lead to a lot of conversions—because obviously, with the type of product WhisperFlow is, it's a bit harder to get students to pay for it. So ultimately we ended up killing the program. I'm not entirely against organic UGC; it's just making sure you're not chasing vanity metrics. And then Tobin did this a lot better at Polymarket—he cracked the code with organic UGC, not just doing very top-of-funnel concepts. But yeah, organic UGC does work. We just didn't see that much success, or the success we wanted, at Whisper. And it was also going to be really hard to find someone to take Tobin's role after he left. So we were like, let's just kill this. And then again, paid was working relatively well for us.
turns.zh: 好，自然 UGC 基本上就是：你把一群创作者聚到一个群里。这些创作者会做关于你产品的视频，然后发在他们自己的 Instagram 主页或 TikTok 主页上。想象一下，你加入了 Whisper 的自然 UGC 群，你建了一个叫 Lenny Whispers 的账号，然后你把自己的视频上传到那里，再按 CPM 指标拿钱。比如，我不知道，每千次观看 2 美元，然后随着观看量越来越高，单价会递减。Tobin 帮我们搭了这套东西，我记得大概两个半月就有 5 亿次观看。CPM 超低，效果还算不错。但我觉得那也是自然 UGC 的早期阶段，大家都非常关注虚荣指标，而这些指标未必带来很多转化——因为显然，WhisperFlow 这类产品，要让学生付费还是有点难。所以最终我们把这个项目砍掉了。我并不完全反对自然 UGC，只是要确保你不是在追逐虚荣指标。后来 Tobin 在 Polymarket 把这件事做得好得多——他破解了自然 UGC 的密码，不只是做非常顶层的概念。但没错，自然 UGC 确实有效，我们只是在 Whisper 没看到那么多成功，或者说没看到我们想要的成功。而且 Tobin 走了之后，也很难找到人接替他的角色。所以我们就想，干脆砍掉吧。再说，付费投放对我们效果相对不错。

turns.en: So that kind of brings us to where we're at now—I mean, not now, but like seven months ago. I realized that paid was working really well, and I was the one making all the paid assets. So I was like, what if we apply Tobin's playbook from organic UGC—building this community, building this roster, and paying off performance—and just apply it to paid? And maybe make the ads a bit more middle-of-funnel, maybe a bit more pitching the product. I mean, not even just middle-of-funnel, because you need everything in paid ads, but more just pitching the product straight on instead of just screen-on-text ads. And then I stumbled upon Tribe—I don't know if you want me to get into that now.
turns.zh: 这就把我们带到了现在——我是说不是现在，而是大概七个月前。我意识到付费投放效果非常好，而所有付费素材都是我在做。所以我就想，如果我们把 Tobin 在自然 UGC 上的打法——建立这个社群、建立这个创作者名册、按效果付费——用到付费投放上会怎样？也许把广告做得更偏中层漏斗一点，也许更多地去推销产品。我是说，甚至不只是中层漏斗，因为付费广告里你什么都需要，但更多是直接推销产品，而不是只做屏幕加文字的广告。然后我偶然发现了 Tribe——不知道你想不想让我现在讲这个。

turns.zh: 因为这是我和很多朋友聊过的最有意思的话题之一，尤其是 Tobin，就像我之前提到的，因为我们俩再相反不过了。如果你把我们的简历并排放在一起，让我问你选哪一个，你脑子里大概会觉得答案很明显，但说到底两个都是正确答案。比如我 GPA 2.5，Tobin 是 4.0。我没上过顶尖名校，Tobin 去了滑铁卢。我打过一级联赛的体育项目，Tobin 没有。有所有这些不同的东西，但最终我们都成了很棒的营销人。可如果你只看简历的表面，这并不明显。不过我觉得 Whisper 很擅长看到一两个真正关键的东西。也能看出：好，这个人适不适合这个文化？看起来是不是很努力？他们的价值观或文化和 Whisper 现有的人是否一致？我觉得 Tenny、Daniel 和团队其他人很擅长不仅发现早期人才、看出该关注哪些关键点，还能看出：好，这是不是一个好人，一个适合加入团队的好人？我觉得 Tobin 和我——当然我可能有点自夸——但我认为我们完美体现了这些性格特质。你可能会问：好，那我招一个好的营销人该看什么特质？说实话，没那么复杂。就是：这个人有没有把一个账号做起来，哪怕只有 1 万粉丝？他们对创作者这件事是不是多少懂行，有没有做过内容？就这么基础。只要他们有建立粉丝群的经验，哪怕粉丝不多，也能说明他们理解把社交媒体粉丝做起来需要怎样的坚持。这说明他们懂趋势、懂怎么做视频、怎么剪辑、怎么拍摄等等。然后，我觉得归根结底是风格。他们看起来是不是努力的人？是不是好人？有没有至少 1 万、1.5 万粉丝？然后就赌一把。而且你不能把一个年轻人招进来就说“好，你没达到我的期望，走人”。Tenny 和 Daniel，还有整个 Whisper 团队，总是给我们很多时间去学习和失败。我确知的是，在 Whisper 的头七个月，我有点——我有点乱七八糟。

turns.en: I still joke about it with Daniel, how there were some hard conversations here and there where you're like, "What's Hector doing?" But yeah, they gave me the freedom to keep experimenting and keep trying new things. And it didn't really matter if you failed as long as you're consistently learning and getting better. And that's the same for Tobin. Tobin came in, they gave him some money and some time to experiment. And after like 2 months, he found something that worked and it stuck.
turns.zh: 我还在和 Daniel 开玩笑说，这里时不时会有一些艰难的对话，你会听到有人说：“Hector 在干什么？”但没错，他们给了我自由去不断尝试和试验新事物。只要你一直在学习、在进步，失败并不重要。Tobin 也是一样。Tobin 加入后，他们给了他一些资金和时间去试验。大约两个月后，他找到了行之有效的方法，并且坚持了下来。

turns.en: I see. What about like X and YouTube?

turns.zh: YouTube 还不错，但我会说如果你理解像 Instagram 这样的平台，你就能攻克任何平台。是的，这就是我的经验。我是说，Instagram 和 YouTube——如果你能攻克 Instagram 和 YouTube，我很有信心，尤其是如果你是个年轻人，你就能攻克任何平台。比如直到两周前我都没怎么在 X 上发过帖。我从 X 上大约 500 粉丝涨到了大约 1.8 万。我其实不太习惯在纯文字平台上发帖，但大约一周后我就搞明白了。就像，好吧，这是一个数量游戏。你需要保持简短，有自己的风格，并且真正提供一些价值。那很容易学。而且我认为如果你从 X 开始，进入视频会有点难，因为视频完全是另一头野兽。坐下来拍摄不是一件容易的事。我有一些同事——我推动他们开始制作视频。向 Eric 致敬。他是我们的媒体采购。我让他制作视频。是的，他在第一个月有点挣扎，但我认为走出舒适区尝试拍摄一些视频是好的。但没错，这绝对不容易。所以我会说是的，Instagram 和 YouTube。

turns.zh: 其实我就是这样在 X 上发现你的，然后它就爆了，现在我的整个信息流最近全是 Hector 的视频。所以我没意识到你两周前才开始发帖。这太疯狂了。显然这又是你在这方面有多高效的另一个标志。所以我想强调的另一点就是年轻人才这个想法。这是你经常谈论的。就是雇佣年轻人的价值，几乎像是阿尔法。

turns.zh: 我想我在很多不同的行业都见过这个例子。我不知道你是否听说过 Jimmy Fairly，但他就像是 TikTok 商店的元老之一。他一直在那里，我不知道，从 17 岁开始。建立了一个庞大的机构。与一些最大的品牌合作。最近我认为他的机构被 Physician's Choice 以大约 200 万美元收购，现在他在他们内部，也和另外两个品牌合作。但我只是看到这个孩子让自己周围——我是说他现在比我大，但我看到他让自己周围都是这些年长的创始人，所有这些电商品牌的年长创始人总是谈论着有一个 Jimmy 在你身边是多么阿尔法，因为一个 30-40 岁的创始人无法理解一个 18 岁的孩子在那些 Discord 聊天中或每天在 Instagram 和 TikTok 上刷屏——他们不理解什么真正有效以及接近这些新渠道的最佳方式。如果你身边有年轻人，无论你在什么行业，无论你是 SaaS、电商还是其他什么，你只是找到一个理解你不理解的事情和早期事物的人，你能够提问并向他们学习，我认为团队中有这样的人是理所当然的。就像即使你现在尽力深入 TikTok 商店或 Tribe，你仍然会挣扎，因为你无法与创作者建立那么多联系，或者你无法理解某些事情，你只是需要更长的时间来适应这些事情，而不是把时间花在你更擅长的事情上，然后带一个能为你管理这些事情的人。

turns.zh: 这是一个奇怪的转变，因为我大约 3 天前也刚刚退出了 Division One 足球。我 literally 回家，在 LinkedIn 上搜索 WhisperFlow。嗯，是的，我想说我在 LinkedIn 上搜索了创作者职位。我申请了大约 200 个职位，找到了一家叫 WhisperFlow 的公司。我申请了，和 Tanay 通了个电话，然后我就加入了。是的，太疯狂了。回顾一些记忆，比如记得那是我们准备发布的最初几天。我当时在我的，我想是微积分课上，Tanay 开始在课上给我发 Slack 消息，我离开去洗手间，打开笔记本电脑，加入了 Slack 通话，他基本上说，‘我们的发布视频不是它应该有的样子。你觉得你能在 CapCut 或你有的任何工具上编辑它，让它更有 Z 世代的氛围吗？’是的，我在上微积分课，我就开始编辑视频。我有一些编辑经验，但 Tanay 在我最初几周就让我做这个，挺吓人的。但是的，这基本上总结了我第一年在 Whisper 的经历。我只是随便捡东西做，没有明确的职位。我 pretty sure 他们也不太知道我在做什么。我也不知道我在做什么。是的，我大概花了一年才真正感到舒适。有很多起起落落。实际上我还想指出一点，我之后还做了一个金融实习。所以，已经一年了。整个学年过去了。然后是我大三升大四，那个夏天我申请了。嗯，我在年初申请了一堆金融实习，因为我不知道内容创作是不是一个真正的职业。显然我很享受 Whisper，我也为我的个人品牌赚了一些不错的钱，但我想，‘我不知道这是不是真正的职业。’我的父母，我们移民到美国等等，我上大学学金融是件大事，他们希望我走传统路线。所以，我最终在纽约市找到了一个金融实习，我平衡着两门暑期课程、WhisperFlow 和金融实习。实习大约 2 周后，我讨厌它。我想，‘我不想要我的生活是这样的。我需要让内容和 Whisper 成功。’所以，我会偷偷溜出办公室，去 Soho 的一些咖啡馆，只是做 Whisper 和我的个人内容。从那时起，一切开始变得顺利，然后是的，差不多就是这样。

turns.en: What a journey. I feel like we could have a whole other conversation about just the creator path and how to become a content creator on Instagram and all these platforms. That's its own thing. I'm going to come back to how you find the creators for this kind of paid UGC strategy.
turns.zh: 多么精彩的旅程。我觉得我们可以另外专门聊一次创作者之路，以及如何在 Instagram 和所有这些平台上成为内容创作者。那是另一个话题。我稍后会回到你如何为这种付费 UGC 策略找到创作者。

turns.en: If we walked through the whole strategy honestly now, I think this would be a good moment to walk through everything. So, yeah, like we were mentioning, the first step is figuring out, okay, if you're in SaaS, you're going to do percent of ad spend. If you're in e-commerce, you're going to do percent of GMV. And then from there, you'll set up the group on whatever platform you choose. I think Tribe is the best one. It's the one we use at Whisper. And then once you have your group set up, it's like, okay, now you have to go actually find the creators. And if you think about it, it's like imagine you're starting a company from zero and you land on a platform and there's thousands of creators, thousands of brands, and your company has no history. More than likely, you're not going to be able to get the best of the best. And this is where a lot of companies go wrong. They'll start doing a lot of outreach on these platforms and they're like, why would a creator want to work for a brand that has no money? For example, on Tribe it says how much money we paid out to creators. It's like $300,000. It says how many creators we have in the group and then how many ads we have running or whatever. And when creators see that we've paid $300,000 out and that we only have 50 creators in, you can imagine the amount of inbound that we get. But on the contrary, if you're a brand who has $0 paid out and zero creators, it's going to be really hard to get creators in. So, what I did is I went off platform and I went on platforms like Instagram. And you just look up a bunch of keywords. It can be like UGC creators, I don't know, tech, 9-to-5, lawyer, doctor, sleep supplements, whatever niche you're in, and just go down a bunch of rabbit holes. And then you'll land on creators that you like, send, and then you also go through their following and follower list and you also search those same exact keywords. Because typically good creators know other good creators. And then I say from around 150 to 250 DMs over a week. And these should be very targeted DMs. It shouldn't be like, 'Oh, I'm going to use some mass software and send 3,000 messages.' Needs to be very—you need to care about the small things because nowadays with all these automations, yes, you can do a lot of things fast, but if you do it very fast, you're probably going to get a lot of slop back or a lot of bad creators back. turns.en: What does the DM look like when you reach out to a creator?
turns.zh: 当你联系创作者时，私信是什么样的？

turns.en: So, it kind of depends and there's honestly some different ways to go about it. A lot of times as a brand, you'll actually have a lot of creators already in your DMs or a lot of creators that are already following you. So, that's like the number one place I would actually start and a lot of our early creators came from there is we would just go into our following list and look up UGC or look up creators. And then also go through our DM requests and you'll actually like come across a lot of creators. And from there, it's like they already follow you, they probably already like your product. So, it gets really easy and you can just be like, "Hey Lenny, I saw your content. I really enjoyed it. Uh I would love to have you be part of our creator group." And I don't necessarily pitch it. I don't necessarily pitch the performance-based thing yet because it's still a pretty it's still a relatively new thing for creators like hearing this new model and a lot of them are skeptical at first, which I understand why. But even like 7 months ago, 6 months ago, it was even more like new. Um so, even then, like today I still wouldn't start with that and like go straight into pitching super hard. I just be like, "Hey, love your content. Would love to have you be part of our creator group. Are you interested?" From there, you'll get a response back. They'll probably ask you for some more details. And then I have like a PDF that's like super simple. I just kind of explain the program structure, how much we pay, how much some of our creators are making. And then from there, I'll just hop on a call with them, close them, and get them like onboarded in Discord, get them WhisperFlow code, and then get them making videos. And the other way is if they don't follow us and I'm doing outreach, is I'll just send them a DM and be like, "Hey, I have somehow across your content. I really enjoyed it. I'd love to have you be part of our WhisperFlow group. This is the tool. This is how it works. Um here's the link to it.
turns.zh: 所以，这取决于情况，老实说有不同的方法。很多时候，作为一个品牌，你的私信里已经有很多创作者，或者很多创作者已经关注你了。所以，这实际上是我会开始的首选地方，我们很多早期创作者都来自那里，我们会进入我们的关注列表，查找 UGC 或查找创作者。然后也浏览我们的私信请求，你实际上会遇到很多创作者。从那里开始，他们已经关注你了，他们可能已经喜欢你的产品。所以变得很容易，你可以直接说：“嘿 Lenny，我看到了你的内容。我很喜欢。我很想让你成为我们创作者小组的一员。”我不一定会推销。我还不一定会推销基于绩效的模式，因为这对创作者来说仍然是一个相对较新的事物，很多人一开始持怀疑态度，我理解为什么。但即使在 7 个月前、6 个月前，它更加新颖。所以，即使今天，我仍然不会一开始就大力推销。我只会说：“嘿，喜欢你的内容。很想让你成为我们创作者小组的一员。你有兴趣吗？”从那里，你会得到回复。他们可能会问你更多细节。然后我有一个非常简单的 PDF。我解释项目结构、我们支付多少、我们一些创作者赚多少。然后，我会和他们通电话，说服他们，让他们加入 Discord，给他们 WhisperFlow 代码，然后让他们制作视频。另一种方式是，如果他们不关注我们，而我在做外联，我会直接发私信说：“嘿，我不知怎么看到了你的内容。我很喜欢。我很想让你成为我们 WhisperFlow 小组的一员。这是工具。这是它如何工作。这是链接。”

turns.en: Let me know if you'd be interested. And then from there, if they're interested again, I'll pitch them and it's kind of the same sort of route.
turns.zh: 如果你感兴趣，请告诉我。然后从那里开始，如果他们再次感兴趣，我会向他们推销，这差不多是同一种路线。

turns.en: And this is from the WhisperFlow Instagram account?
turns.zh: 这是来自 WhisperFlow 的 Instagram 账号吗？

turns.en: Sometimes I do either or because I also so since I'm a creator myself, I also I a lot of I do which is also the pros of hiring people who are in content. Some of our best hires at Whisper in content have been through me posting on Instagram stories or our best creator hires. I'll be like, "Hey, I'm looking for UGC creators." Just post a story. Or hey, I'm looking for a videographer. Or hey, I'm looking for an editor. Like that's one of the cool things about hiring a content creator. Um if if they make again content and and you just make sure they make high value content is they can also be used as like a very good hiring mechanism. And yeah. It depends. Like if if you have someone who's a creator, I think it works pretty well. Um you obviously you get creator face, whatever. And then also if you're a really well-known brand, obviously if your creator getting a message from like Nike or whatever, you know what I mean? Like it it's very impressive and you're probably more likely to get a response. I think it just depends.
turns.zh: 有时我会两者都做，因为我自己也是创作者，所以我经常做的一件事，这也是雇佣内容创作者的好处之一。我们在 Whisper 的一些最佳内容招聘都是通过我在 Instagram 故事上发布信息实现的，或者是我们最好的创作者招聘。我会说：“嘿，我正在寻找 UGC 创作者。”只需发一个故事。或者嘿，我正在寻找摄像师。或者嘿，我正在寻找编辑。就像雇佣内容创作者的一个很酷的事情是，如果他们再次制作内容，你只需确保他们制作高价值内容，他们也可以被用作一个非常好的招聘机制。是的，这取决于情况。如果你有一个创作者，我认为效果很好。你显然会得到创作者的面孔，等等。然后，如果你是一个知名品牌，显然如果你的创作者收到像耐克之类的消息，你懂我的意思吗？这非常令人印象深刻，你更有可能得到回复。我认为这取决于情况。

turns.en: And then okay, so you DM them, they're interested, you send them kind of an overview. In the early say the first five, you say you hop on a call pretty quickly and just kind of pitch them and explain the program. What's like downboarding look like?
turns.zh: 然后好的，所以你私信他们，他们感兴趣，你给他们发送一个概述。在早期，比如说前五个，你说你很快会打电话给他们，只是推销并解释这个项目。那么“下行引导”是什么样的？

turns.en: These creators are very used to just being used and like just it's everything they do is like a transaction. They make a video, they get paid, and they never talk to a person again. And we live in a like day and age where everything is digital, everything's virtual. Most people are working remote, most creators are remote, and they crave community on the same way just like a regular person would crave community. And we just make sure like that we connect from the get-go and like it's like at the end they're just like friends. We're like working together. I don't see them as just like, "Hey, a creator that I'm going to extract some videos from and never talk to again." I get on a call with them, like you said, and I have this whole slideshow, but before I go to my slideshow, I like ask them about themselves, like how they got into content, why they enjoy it, and just like have a conversation. Try to get to know them. And then from there the flow of the of the slideshow is I have an intro slide where I talk about myself. I talk about my background as a creator, so like they respect me and they know I'm not just some random dude talking to them. Um and then from there I'll also intro our media buyer, who's Eric. Shout out to Eric. And then from there I explain the product. And then from there I explain how Tribe works. So I like it I let them know like what they can expect in terms of the flow from them making the video to it getting accepted to it getting run as an ad. I tell them we pay them out every 7 days, which is like another um hack as well. Like you want to keep your creators motivated and the higher the dopamine rush they can get and the more money you can get them early on, the better. Um so, yeah, we pay out 7 days. We tell them that. Then from there, we show them some example ads and then I get them onboarded and fully going on the call. It's almost like you're closing you're closing like a sales deal. You don't want to get them all excited and then you let them get off and then you have to chase them down. It's like you want to be very um strategic with your time and their time. So, I try to like meet them, introduce myself, get them onboarded, and get them going so that they know like, "Hey, you can start making a video right now."
turns.zh: 这些创作者非常习惯于被利用，就像他们所做的一切都是一笔交易。他们制作一个视频，得到报酬，然后再也不和任何人交谈。我们生活在一个数字化的时代，一切都是虚拟的。大多数人在远程工作，大多数创作者在远程工作，他们渴望社区，就像普通人渴望社区一样。我们只是确保从一开始就建立联系，就像最后他们就像朋友一样。我们就像在合作。我不把他们仅仅看作“嘿，一个创作者，我要从中提取一些视频，然后再也不和他说话。”我和他们通电话，就像你说的，我有整个幻灯片，但在进入幻灯片之前，我会问他们关于自己的问题，比如他们如何进入内容创作，为什么喜欢它，就像聊天一样。试着了解他们。然后从那里开始，幻灯片的流程是我有一个介绍幻灯片，我谈论自己。我谈论我作为创作者的背景，这样他们尊重我，知道我不是随便一个家伙在和他们说话。然后从那里，我还会介绍我们的媒体购买员，他是 Eric。向 Eric 致敬。然后从那里我解释产品。然后从那里我解释 Tribe 如何运作。所以我让他们知道从制作视频到被接受再到作为广告运行的过程中可以期待什么。我告诉他们我们每 7 天付款一次，这也是另一个窍门。你想保持创作者的积极性，他们能获得的 dopamine 冲动越高，你早期能给他们越多钱，就越好。所以，是的，我们 7 天付款。我们告诉他们这一点。然后从那里，我们展示一些广告示例，然后我在通话中让他们入职并完全开始。这几乎就像你在完成一笔销售交易。你不想让他们兴奋起来，然后让他们离开，然后你不得不追赶他们。就像你想在时间和他们的时间上非常有策略。所以，我试着与他们见面，介绍自己，让他们入职并开始，这样他们就知道：“嘿，你现在就可以开始制作视频了。”

turns.en: So, big lesson here is treat them treat them like humans. Care about them, help them feel like they're part of this thing, not just feel like you're okay, you're going to make money. Just shut up, don't worry about it. You're going to make money.
turns.zh: 所以，这里的大教训是像对待人一样对待他们。关心他们，帮助他们感觉自己是这件事的一部分，而不仅仅是感觉你没问题，你会赚钱。闭嘴，别担心。你会赚钱的。

turns.en: And I think this is actually really good alpha as well. So, I think the companies that will win long-term are the companies that have the best relationships with creators because words word gets out really fast. And if you're a brand that treats creators bad, doesn't pay on time, doesn't pay them whatsoever maybe or you just block them, etc., word will get out and creators probably won't want to work with you or you won't get the best terms or you won't get the best quality creators. Um so, I think one really big thing we focus on at not even just with creators, but any external agencies or anyone we work with, we always want to treat everyone with a lot of respect. Um and and yeah, I think I think it's the companies that do that the best will will win long-term as well.
turns.zh: 我认为这实际上也是非常好的 alpha。所以，我认为长期获胜的公司将是与创作者关系最好的公司，因为消息传得很快。如果你是一个对待创作者不好的品牌，不按时付款，或者根本不付款，或者你只是屏蔽他们等等，消息会传开，创作者可能不想和你合作，或者你不会得到最好的条件，或者你不会得到最优质的创作者。所以，我认为我们在不仅仅与创作者，而且与任何外部机构或任何我们合作的人身上关注的一件非常重要的事情是，我们总是希望以极大的尊重对待每个人。嗯，是的，我认为做得最好的公司也会长期获胜。

turns.en: What does the early team look like to start this initiative? Is it just A Hector that is running this solo or is there a larger team that you'd start with?
turns.zh: 启动这个计划的早期团队是什么样的？是只有 Hector 一个人独自运营，还是有更大的团队一起启动？

turns.en: Honestly, it's it's pretty lean. So, our marketing team as a whole is pretty flat. Obviously, we're growing a bit faster now at Wispri. I think we've passed like 120 full-time employees now, which is pretty crazy. Um because I joined I think we were like four at the time. I I remember mess- I messaged Snae the other day. I was at the office and I was like, "Holy cow, like I just had like a a moment where I was like, there's so many people around like this is crazy blah blah but yeah right now we're pretty lean team and we were even more lean before but for tribe specifically to get something like this running all you really need is someone like me to kind of be the comms with creators come up with new concepts approve videos kind of get everything kickstarted and then you need a media buyer it's pretty rare to find someone who's a creative and also media buyer I don't really like numbers that much I'm not really much of a numbers guy and I don't like staring at meta ads manager I've heard it's a headache so I'm happy I don't have to do that but yeah we have Eric on the media buying side of things and he like structures our ad account and everything
turns.zh: 老实说，团队相当精简。所以我们的营销团队整体上相当扁平。显然，我们现在在 Wispri 增长得有点快。我想我们现在已经超过了 120 名全职员工，这相当疯狂。因为我加入时，我想我们大概只有四个人。我记得前几天我给 Snae 发了消息。我在办公室，我说：“天哪，我刚才有一刻觉得周围这么多人，这太疯狂了等等，但是的，现在我们团队相当精简，之前甚至更精简，但具体对于 Tribe 来说，要让这样的项目运行起来，你真正需要的只是一个像我这样的人来与创作者沟通，想出新的概念，批准视频，启动一切，然后你需要一个媒体购买员。找到一个既是创意人又是媒体购买员的人相当罕见。我不太喜欢数字，我不是一个数字型的人，我不喜欢盯着 Meta 广告管理器，我听说那很头疼，所以我很高兴我不必做那个，但是的，我们有 Eric 负责媒体购买方面，他构建我们的广告账户等等。

turns.en: So when this media buyer is this kind of like a performance marketing person that just lives in Facebook's ad system or
turns.zh: 所以这个媒体购买员是那种只生活在 Facebook 广告系统中的绩效营销人员吗，或者

turns.en: Yeah exactly so yeah yeah Eric's basically just lives in our on the media buying side of things on Facebook LinkedIn YouTube etc.
turns.zh: 是的，没错，所以是的，Eric 基本上就生活在我们的媒体购买方面，在 Facebook、LinkedIn、YouTube 等平台上。

turns.en: Got it. So you're kind of like the creative, you're like the content supply, and then this person takes it and then is responsible for running the ads, watching performance, so optimizing the spend. Got it. Okay. And then is there anyone else that you find important, valuable on that team early on and even later on?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你有点像创意人员，你负责内容供应，然后这个人接手，负责投放广告、监控表现，从而优化支出。明白了。好的。那么早期和后期，你觉得团队里还有哪些重要、有价值的人？

turns.en: Early, like if we go back to the early early days, the marketing team was Daniel, our CMO, Matt, who was our head of growth before Eric came, and then it was me, just like as a sole creator kind of just making the ads myself. So and then we had some external agencies here and there. And then slowly we added on design, we added on an in-house like director and how to produce films and launch videos. Then we introduced like PR recently. And like even even now, I think we're still pretty lean. I think we might be like 15 people on the marketing team like full-time. We have a creative partnership leads for like influencers. We have a celebrity talent manager that helps us close celebrities and and things like that. So even then it's it's still pretty lean and everyone is like experts in their domain and it's all very flat. We all just have free reign. We all do what we're best at. There's no real There's no really middle management. And then our our poor CMO Daniel, who's an absolute legend, he just had a bunch of direct reports. Um so, I feel sorry for his calendar, but yeah, that's that's kind of how everything is structured. It's like very flat. No middle managers. Everyone just does their work.
turns.zh: 早期，如果我们回到最初的日子，营销团队是 Daniel，我们的首席营销官，Matt，在 Eric 来之前是我们的增长负责人，然后就是我，作为一个独立创作者，自己制作广告。所以，然后我们时不时有一些外部机构。然后慢慢地我们增加了设计，增加了内部导演，负责制作影片和发布视频。然后我们最近引入了公关。而且即使现在，我认为我们仍然相当精简。我想营销团队可能有 15 个全职人员。我们有创意合作负责人负责影响者。我们有名人人才经理帮助我们签约名人等等。所以即使那样，它仍然相当精简，每个人都是自己领域的专家，而且非常扁平。我们都有自由支配权。我们都做自己最擅长的事。没有真正的没有真正的中层管理。然后我们可怜的 CMO Daniel，他绝对是个传奇，他有一堆直接下属。嗯，所以，我为他的日历感到难过，但是的，这就是结构。非常扁平。没有中层管理者。每个人都只是做自己的工作。

turns.en: Is a core kind of takeaway from this conversation that when you're doing paid today, that UGC videos are the way to go versus your own ads that you're just kind of creating?
turns.zh: 这次对话的一个核心要点是，如今做付费广告时，UGC 视频是正确的方式，而不是你自己制作的广告？

turns.en: So, are you kind of comparing to like what I was doing versus what we're doing now?
turns.zh: 所以，你是在比较我以前做的和我们现在的做法吗？

turns.en: You know, just like when you think paid ads on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, most people think I create a video promoting my product or create like an ad unit that is, "Hey, Whisper Floss is the best thing." And what you're doing here is you're having other people create the videos and then running that as the ad.
turns.zh: 你知道，就像当你想在 Facebook、Instagram、TikTok 上做付费广告时，大多数人认为我制作一个推广产品的视频，或者创建一个广告单元，说“嘿，Whisper Floss 是最好的东西。”而你在这里做的是让其他人制作视频，然后将其作为广告投放。

turns.en: Yeah. So, the way I look at it is like I was basically an in-house UGC creator. And it got to a point where ad spend was getting too high and like I'm only human and I couldn't I couldn't make that many videos and it was also getting into like a year plus of making ads. So, naturally I was getting pretty burnt out being a one-man show and like I was like, "Okay, I have the skill set. I'm a decent creator. I can spot like good creators as well. Why not just build a team and that's like an extension of myself?" And yeah, that's that's basically what we did and we're able to scale a lot faster, test more ideas since we have more ad spend, we obviously want more concepts running. And also, like once you get to a pretty high budget on ads, your ads are typically going to reach fatigue a lot faster. And especially with Andromeda now, ads reach fatigue even a lot faster cuz before then 2024 when we were running ads, I could have an ad running for 12 months and I mean, my my output would be a lot less, but now an ad with not only the new updates, but also how much ad spend we're running, an ad once it hits like $100,000 in ad spend, will be dead and that can be hit in like a month or 2 weeks, 3 weeks. So, we constantly need more output, more volume, etc. And I think that if you look at our ad library, we might have like 5,000 lifetime ads, and maybe like 800 live currently or something like that, or 900 live currently. And it's because again, they reach fatigue, and then we have to turn them off. But, our ad our ad set or our ad library isn't only full of UGC videos. There's a lot of different things as well. turns.zh: 是的，我想这基本上概括了。还有另一条我最近发的、我很有共鸣的推文，是关于招聘的体育视角。运动队——我来自一个竞争非常激烈的体育背景。我在西班牙踢过球，我为拉科鲁尼亚的拉利加青训营踢过球，我在美国踢过 MLS Next，我在大学踢过一级联赛。我们有一套完整的体育队体系：你考察年轻人才，把他们带进来，指导他们，培养他们十年。然后，如果你在西班牙或欧洲，你最终会把他们纳入你的青训营，也许是二队，然后也许把他们卖给顶级俱乐部。或者他们最终成为本土合同球员，加入你的第一队。我认为很多初创公司应该采用这种心态。我觉得很多公司实际上不再做实习项目了。他们认为实习没有价值。而我认为实习是最有价值的事情之一，如果你能找到合适的人，这并不昂贵，也不耗时。嗯，是的，我认为给年轻人一个机会，给他们一些钱去尝试，给他们一些自由去尝试，允许他们失败并继续学习，这是你可以从体育中借鉴的最好的模式之一。显然这行得通——我不知道你是否很熟悉足球，但看看拉明·亚马尔，他刚赢得世界杯，才 19 岁、18 岁。我认为同样的方法可以应用到初创界：找到年轻人才，投资他们，让他们在现实世界获得真正的锻炼，最终他们可能会成为你的 A 级球员。

turns.en: I love that. Uh and I love that also part of this is giving them time to figure it out.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。我也喜欢其中一部分是给他们时间去摸索。

turns.en: What's really interesting about this conversation so far I'm realizing is I don't think we've once mentioned AI as a part of this work that you do which is really interesting because it's you know it's it's all anyone talks about these days and you actually had this tweet the other day the best marketers are allergic to AI. Talk about just what you what you think with how AI plays into this and how AI should not play into this.
turns.zh: 我意识到到目前为止这次对话真正有趣的是，我想我们一次都没提到 AI 作为你工作的一部分，这真的很有趣，因为你知道这是现在所有人都在谈论的。你前几天实际上发了这条推文：最好的市场营销人员对 AI 过敏。谈谈你对 AI 如何融入其中以及 AI 不应如何融入其中的看法。

turns.en: I just think like overall when you look at a lot of the work done like even like looking at the top labs like they are some of the people that have the most amount of humans actually working on a specific asset and like maybe yes they have a lot of the research automated or a lot of different steps like internally automated but the actual production of the asset whether it comes to the video the design in Figma um the editing the post production etc. it's all done by teams of a lot of humans and I think there's not going to be a real way to get around on that at least not anytime soon and especially in like the environment we're in now where a lot of people are very I guess turned off by AI and it can be a scary like thing to talk about. If you're an AI company like Whisper who in theory we enable humans to do better work we don't want to replace anyone's job want to give them I guess the tools to be able to be more productive to do more work and to sound more naturally and to sound like themselves more naturally. If we on the other side go out and start making AI slop ads and videos with AI influencers and I don't know AI designs and AI statics, it's probably not going to be received really well and it just it looks off and like when I say that I think it goes more towards not automating the work that's going to be the final product that people are looking at. Um, because I think you see it a lot of times like it'll it'll end up blowing back on on the companies where whether it's like an animation that they made with Claude or um, some sort of asset that they made and maybe there's typos or maybe the writing is like all jumbled up like what happens when you do it with with open it with chat GPT or whatever. Um, and yeah, I think it's it's not worth it. Like the risk versus reward is not worth it.
turns.zh: 我只是觉得，总的来说，当你审视很多完成的工作时，甚至看看顶级实验室，他们实际上是让最多人类实际参与特定资产制作的人。也许是的，他们有很多研究自动化了，或者很多不同步骤在内部自动化了，但实际资产的生产——无论是视频、Figma 中的设计、编辑、后期制作等——都是由大量人类团队完成的。我认为这一点无法真正绕过，至少短期内不会，尤其是在我们现在所处的环境中，很多人对 AI 感到反感，谈论它可能很可怕。如果你是一家像 Whisper 这样的 AI 公司，理论上我们让人类做更好的工作，我们不想取代任何人的工作，而是想给他们工具，让他们更高效、做更多工作、听起来更自然、更像他们自己。如果我们另一方面开始制作 AI 垃圾广告、用 AI 网红制作视频、AI 设计、AI 静态图，可能不会得到很好的反响，看起来就不对。当我说这些时，我认为更多是指不要自动化那些将成为人们看到的最终产品的工作。因为我觉得你经常看到这种情况，最终会反噬公司——无论是他们用 Claude 制作的动画，还是他们制作的某种资产，也许有错别字，或者文字乱七八糟，就像你用 ChatGPT 打开时发生的那样。嗯，是的，我认为不值得。风险与回报不成正比。

turns.en: So the alpha what I'm hearing here is like don't use AI for this work.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的精华是：不要在这项工作中使用 AI。

turns.en: Yeah, for for the final output especially on the creative side like what other people are going to see I I don't think AI should should touch yet.
turns.zh: 是的，尤其是最终输出，特别是创意方面，别人会看到的东西，我认为 AI 还不应该碰。

turns.en: That is really interesting. Like, you know, people it feels like everyone's hearing leaning to AI.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。你知道，感觉每个人都在转向 AI。

turns.en: Yeah. Even even even one of the most bullish people on AI that I know, um, Matt who is now at at Victor or exited growth, he has the most automations I've ever seen in the whole wide world, but even then like that last um, like 10% that's the most important always has a human on the endpoint because you can't sacrifice as a brand having something blow up because you had something screw up or come out wrong or or whatever. And yeah, I think with everyone I think with everyone also just shipping so much volume and like whether it be on X, on LinkedIn, on Instagram, on YouTube, like you're able now to make videos with Claude, you're able to to have the edited them, you're able to make um, what's it called? You're able to make like a doppelganger of yourself with AI and and all these different things and get content out faster and have these automations for tweets and have it like post news articles and whatever and retweet it in whatever way.
turns.zh: 是的。甚至我认识的最看好 AI 的人之一，Matt，他现在在 Victor 或 exited growth，他拥有我见过的最多的自动化，但即使如此，最后那 10% 最重要的部分总是有人在终点把关，因为作为一个品牌，你不能牺牲，不能因为某件事搞砸了或出错了就爆掉。是的，我认为每个人——每个人也都在发布大量内容，无论是在 X、LinkedIn、Instagram、YouTube 上，你现在可以用 Claude 制作视频，可以编辑它们，可以制作——叫什么来着？你可以用 AI 制作自己的分身等等，更快地发布内容，有推文的自动化，让它发布新闻文章之类的，并以任何方式转发。

turns.en: There's so much noise. Like you're saying, if you actually focus more on the quality and less on the quantity, and less on building all these crazy automations and hitting volume just for volume's sake, it gets so easy to cut through the noise. So if you actually have real value, you package it well, and you post—not a lot—you post with purpose and for an actual reason, you can cut through really easily as a brand or as a company. I think another good example of this is also our YouTube channel. We started it around—what—three months ago, and five YouTube videos in, we're at millions and millions of views, 20,000 or 21,000 subscribers on YouTube, which is one of the hardest platforms to grow. A lot of people think, oh, we're starting a YouTube channel, we need to post three videos a week. And it's like, no. If you actually put in the time and effort, and you tell a really good story, and you do everything with purpose, and you package it really well, and you have a really good team of humans actually touching everything in there, you get a really good end product, and people can actually see the effort you put into it.
turns.zh: 噪音太多了。就像你说的，如果你真正把重心放在质量而非数量上，少去搞那些花里胡哨的自动化、少为了走量而走量，穿透噪音就会变得非常容易。所以如果你真的有真实价值，把它包装好，而且你发得不多——你带着目的、有真正理由地去发——那么作为品牌或公司，你很容易就能穿透噪音。我觉得另一个很好的例子是我们的 YouTube 频道。我们大概三个月前开始做，发了五条视频就达到了数百万的播放量，YouTube 上有两万或两万一千订阅者，而 YouTube 是最难增长的平台之一。很多人觉得，哦，我们要开 YouTube 频道了，得一周发三条视频。但其实不是。如果你真正投入时间和精力，讲一个好故事，做每件事都有目的，包装得非常好，而且有一个很棒的真人团队去打磨每一个细节，你就会得到非常好的成品，人们也真的能看到你投入的心血。

turns.en: That's actually where I was going to go, and this could be our final thread to chat through—just this other lever, which is, I don't know if you just call it founder-led growth, or—
turns.zh: 这正好是我要聊的方向，这也可以作为我们最后聊的一条线——就是另一个杠杆，我不知道你是不是就叫它创始人驱动的增长，还是——

turns.en: Yeah, founder-led content.
turns.zh: 对，创始人驱动的内容。

turns.en: Founder-led content. Just give us a sense of that growth opportunity, what you're seeing there—the opportunity to drive growth for your product through founder-led content.
turns.zh: 创始人驱动的内容。给我们讲讲这个增长机会，你看到了什么——通过创始人驱动的内容为你的产品驱动增长的机会。

turns.en: Yeah, I think it also ties into what we just talked about—so much AI, so much ads and companies, etc. And at the end of the day, it also ties back to everything in content, creator, and people. At the end of the day, people buy from people, people invest in people. And I think having a founder who can put his face out there, can talk on camera, you can use in ads, you can use to tell the story, it makes the company and the product feel that much more human. When you compare two products—even from my own experience, if I follow, I don't know, let's say I follow George Heaton, who's the founder of Represent, he has a clothing brand. And then there's another ad that I see for a clothing brand, I'm much more likely to buy the product—George's product—because I know how he works. I know his routine. I know the type of person he is. I know what he stands for. I know how hard he works for his company and what he actually puts into it. And I think people really appreciate that, and again, in such a digital age, being able to connect with the founder behind the product. You not only create superfans—people who already use your product but now also love you—you also bring in this new group of people who have never seen your product, they don't really know who you are, and then slowly they start to like the content you're putting out. They start to buy into the mission. They start to buy into the company. And then they actually try the product. And it's this long-horizon type play—I don't know, this long-term play that you have to make, and it's an investment, because you can't just start a YouTube channel or a founder-led brand and instantly start selling at people, because people are just going to switch off and be like, okay, I don't want to be part of this anymore. But if you just give a lot of value, you overshare, you overdeliver, and you just open up the doors into what the culture is like, what you're building, people really appreciate that, and you get them to buy in and drop their guards. And then maybe a year in, we actually maybe have a soft sell. Maybe we have like, hey guys, here's some support—thanks for getting us 100,000 subscribers, just want to drop this code, blah blah. And then people want to support you. So I think again, in this world where everyone's just trying to get instant growth and everything's super fast and optimize everything from the start, these channels that maybe don't have any direct correlations in the present moment end up being some of the best long-term plays and also brand-building plays.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这也和我们刚聊的内容相关——现在 AI 太多了、广告太多了、公司也太多了。归根结底，这又回到内容、创作者和人身上。说到底，人是向人买东西的，人是向人投资的。我觉得有一个创始人能把自己的脸露出来、能对着镜头讲话、能用在广告里、能用来讲故事，会让公司和产品显得有人情味得多。当你比较两个产品时——甚至从我自己的经历来说，如果我关注了，比如说，我关注了 Represent 的创始人 George Heaton，他有一个服装品牌。然后我又看到另一个服装品牌的广告，我会更愿意买 George 的产品，因为我知道他是怎么工作的。我知道他的日常。我知道他是什么样的人。我知道他代表什么。我知道他为公司有多努力、真正投入了什么。我觉得人们真的很欣赏这一点，而且在这个如此数字化的时代，能够和产品背后的创始人建立连接。你不仅创造了超级粉丝——那些已经在用你产品的人现在也爱上了你——你还带来了这一群从未见过你产品、不太认识你的人，然后慢慢地他们开始喜欢你发布的内容。他们开始认同这个使命。他们开始认同这家公司。然后他们真的去试用产品。这是一种长周期的打法——一种你必须做的长期布局，它是一种投资，因为你不能刚开个 YouTube 频道或创始人品牌就立刻向人推销，因为人们会直接关掉，觉得，好吧，我不想再参与这个了。但如果你只是提供大量价值，你过度分享、超额交付，你打开大门让人看到文化是什么样的、你在构建什么，人们真的很欣赏，你让他们认同并放下戒备。然后也许一年后，我们才真正来一次软性推销。也许我们会说，嘿大家，这里有些支持——感谢你们让我们达到 10 万订阅，只想发个优惠码，等等。然后人们就会想要支持你。所以我觉得，在这个人人都想立刻增长、一切都超快、从一开始就优化一切的世界里，这些也许在当下没有直接关联的频道，最终会成为最好的长期布局，也是最好的品牌建设布局。

turns.en: What are some of the angles, slash stories, that seem to work well when you're doing this sort of founder-led content? Is it like, here's the story of our company?
turns.zh: 做这种创始人驱动的内容时，哪些角度或故事似乎效果比较好？是那种“这是我们公司的故事”吗？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Is there anything there?
turns.zh: 这里面有什么门道吗？

turns.en: So the way we kind of thought about it at Whisper is—at Whisper, honestly, at any company—every company is going to have some sort of story or some sort of mission that they're building towards. For us at Whisper, it's getting to 1 billion daily active users. And that's everything—everything we do at Whisper is to get towards that goal. And when we look at the content we make, everything needs to play back into that story. It's almost like you're building this Netflix series where each episode is obviously going to be different, but it all ties back into the overarching theme. Whether you're building in medicine or dev tools or whatever it is, there's going to be some sort of mission that you're chasing as a company. And you want to bring people along for that ride. And if you tie that into every episode or into every LinkedIn post, every X post—obviously the formatting and the messaging is different on every platform—but if you tie all of this together, it brings everyone along for the journey, and it makes it a lot easier to grasp, and also a lot easier to build off of, because you're like, okay, this is the vision, this is what we're building towards, and this is how each step actually leads us to that. It's our mission. It's almost like a physical representation of a product roadmap or what's actually happening to the company—showing it on display to the world, the ups, the downs, the struggles, everything. That's kind of how we think about it at Whisper, and how I think other companies should think about it as well.
turns.zh: 我们在 Whisper 是这样想的——在 Whisper，说实话在任何公司都一样——每家公司都会有某种故事或某种正在为之努力的使命。对我们 Whisper 来说，就是达到 10 亿日活跃用户。那就是一切——我们在 Whisper 做的每件事都是为了朝那个目标前进。当我们看我们制作的内容时，一切都必须回扣到那个故事上。这几乎就像你在打造一部 Netflix 剧集，每一集显然都会不同，但都回扣到 overarching 的主题上。无论你是在做医疗、开发工具还是别的什么，作为公司你都会在追寻某种使命。你想带着人们一起踏上这段旅程。如果你把这一点贯穿到每一集、每一条 LinkedIn 帖子、每一条 X 帖子——显然每个平台的格式和表达方式都不同——但如果你把这一切串起来，它就能带着大家一起走上这段旅程，也让人更容易理解，也更容易在此基础上继续构建，因为你会觉得，好，这就是愿景，这就是我们在构建的东西，而每一步是如何真正带我们走向那里的。这是我们的使命。它几乎就像是产品路线图或公司实际发生的事情的一种实体呈现——向世界展示它，高潮、低谷、挣扎，一切。这就是我们在 Whisper 的思考方式，也是我认为其他公司应该采用的思考方式。

turns.en: That's awesome advice. Basically, have a North Star, like a North Star metric that you're chasing.
turns.zh: 这建议太棒了。基本上就是有一个北极星，一个你在追寻的北极星指标。

turns.en: Yeah. And the journey there, and things you're learning.
turns.zh: 对。还有通往那里的旅程，以及你学到的东西。

turns.en: Things that are surprising. And we'll point people to the channel to give them a sense of what you're actually doing there.
turns.zh: 那些令人意外的东西。我们会把大家引向那个频道，让他们了解你们在那里实际在做什么。

turns.en: Yeah, it's just Tanay Kothari, and yeah, we just document everything on there—the episodes. We've basically done everything from showing how we launched our new product Note Taker, to Tanay going to India and doing wedding shopping, and also working remote and how he balances that and his relationship with Sahaj, to just a week in the life of a founder.
turns.zh: 对，就是 Tanay Kothari，对，我们就在上面记录一切——那些剧集。我们基本上什么都做了，从展示我们如何发布新产品 Note Taker，到 Tanay 去印度置办婚礼用品，还有远程工作以及他如何平衡这些和与 Sahaj 的关系，再到创始人一周的生活。

turns.en: We also did a whiteboard breakdown where I spoke with Tanay. And it's like all these different formats that all might feel different and look different, but they end up building towards this bigger vision of what Whispers building towards.
turns.zh: 我们还做了一次白板讲解，我和 Tanay 聊了聊。所有这些不同的形式可能感觉不同、看起来也不同，但它们最终都朝着 Whisper 正在构建的更大愿景迈进。

turns.en: I imagine there's already some innate interest in Whisper Flow by when you started it. It's like a company people when they see it, they're like, 'Oh, I want to.'
turns.zh: 我想当你开始做 Whisper Flow 时，已经有一些内在的兴趣了。就像一家公司，人们看到它时，他们会说：‘哦，我想要。’

turns.en: So, there's probably a bit of like you can't start that from the beginning when no one cares about what the no one cares what you've learned cuz no one cares about your company yet.
turns.zh: 所以，可能有一点像：你无法从一开始就做到那样，因为没人关心你学到了什么，因为还没人关心你的公司。

turns.en: I honestly think you can start it though. But like maybe it put us in a bit better of a position, but I mean there's founders who don't have as brands as big as Whisper who have found success with personal brand content. And again, it's like a gateway into the actual brand. And it's like what easier way to make that accessible than through a person who's just telling their story and getting value.
turns.zh: 不过，我真心认为你可以开始做。但也许这让我们处于稍微更好的位置，但我的意思是，有些创始人的品牌没有 Whisper 那么大，他们也通过个人品牌内容取得了成功。再说，这就像是进入实际品牌的一个入口。还有什么比通过一个讲述自己故事并获得价值的人更容易让人接触呢？

turns.en: And so interestingly, this is just another, let's say, alpha opportunity to grow, which is the founder sharing their story in a really compelling way.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这只是另一个，比如说，增长的 alpha 机会，即创始人以非常引人入胜的方式分享他们的故事。

turns.en: And you see like everything starts to tie in as well because the more places you show up organically and the more touch points you have with the customer, the cheaper it's going to get when it comes to paid because what is it? I think a customer needs to a person needs to see a piece of content of a company like seven times before they actually make a purchase. If you're able to hit them on YouTube long form, which is a bunch of trust built up since it's a long form platform and then you're also posting Instagram reels from the founder. You're also posting on LinkedIn. Then when they get to my on the first ad they see, they're going to convert. So like I think these organic channels work hand in hand with paid. Like the more that you have activated and the more you have running, the cheaper all the conversions get across all platforms.
